title: How high-hope leadership prepares organizations for uncertainty https://www.smartbrief.com/original/how-high-hope-leadership-prepares-organizations-for-uncertainty
author: Nikolas Badminton
summary: Futurist Nikolas Badminton argues that most leadership teams suffer less from a strategy problem than from a poverty of imagination and a deficit of anticipation. His alternative is a high-hope mindset, grounded in C.R. Snyder's hope theory of agency and pathways and combined with futures work to show where effort will matter most. He illustrates the approach with a client who staged a planned investment in Spain over three years after climate scenarios showed the region facing heat stress. Badminton then lists eight daily practices, from starting the day with a sentence of purpose and asking hopeful questions to slowing one decision per day and practicing speculative gratitude. He closes by describing Hope Engineers as leaders who pair imagination, anticipation and empathy with practical delivery.
points: Hope is defined as a practical discipline of agency and pathways, not wishful thinking or optimism.
High-hope people generate more alternatives and recover from adversity, while low-hope people see barriers and lose motivation.
Writing down a goal with three possible routes to it is offered as a simple way to restore momentum when blocked.
Deliberately slowing one decision each day counters the speed that undermines intentional leadership.
quotes: Most leadership teams are still running a 2000s operating system: growth at any cost, quarter by quarter. It isn’t a strategy problem. It’s a poverty of imagination and a deficit of anticipation

They called an emergency meeting of their operations executives and staged the investment over three years rather than committing upfront. Hope didn’t make them optimistic. It made them look further ahead.

High-hope leaders use six activities to gain understanding and drive execution: reflection, futures thinking, goal setting, pathway building, actions and agency recognition. This work builds on C.R. Snyder’s hope theory, which identifies agency and pathways as the two engines of hopeful action.

Practice pathways thinking. When you hit resistance, write down the goal and three possible ways to move toward it. Simply seeing alternative routes increases agency and momentum, which in turn reinforces hope.

Slow down one decision per day. Choose one decision due that day and deliberately slow it down. Take three breaths. Reread the inputs. Ask, “What futures does this decision invite?” Speed is the enemy of intentionality.
It’s no small feat to build a hopeful mindset, drive transformation toward better futures and champion large-scale change. It takes stamina and ongoing maintenance
It’s about finding possibilities and meeting them with practical delivery, with hope as the energy for change.
